kurz: Where price pressure comes from, why the same money supply creates inflation on one occasion and not on another, and why falling prices are more dangerous than rising ones.

bloecke.md:
Saying that “money is losing value” does not explain rising prices. It describes the result and not the cause. Inflation arises when demand backed by the ability to pay meets a supply that cannot keep up, or when production costs rise from outside. Which case applies matters in practice, because it determines whether a central bank should respond and whether it can do anything about the trigger at all.

## Three sources of inflation

Demand pull arises when incomes, credit or government spending grow faster than production capacity. The labour market is then tight, order books are full, and companies can push through price increases without losing customers. Cost push works from the supply side. Wages, intermediate inputs, energy or taxes make production more expensive, and prices rise even though the economy is weak. Imported inflation is a special case of cost push in which the trigger lies abroad, for example in oil, gas, freight rates or a depreciating exchange rate.

bloecke.md: The composition of the inflation rate shows which type is at work. In August 2026 the German consumer price index was 2.9% higher than in the same month of the previous year. Behind this were fuels at +27.7% and energy as a whole at +10.5%. Food was practically unchanged at +0.1%, and the core rate excluding energy and food was 2.4%. In the USA the gap in the same month was even larger, with a headline rate of 3.4% and a core rate of 2.4%. There, the headline rate was a full percentage point above domestic price pressure. This pattern is the hallmark of a supply shock and not of an overheating economy.

bloecke.titel: Price increases by category in Germany, August 2026
bloecke.unter: The headline rate of 2.9% is made up of, among other things, +27.7% for fuels and +0.1% for food, and it is an average that does not exactly reflect the price trend of any individual household.

serien.name: Change on the same month a year earlier

bloecke.md: The headline rate and the core rate answer different questions. The headline rate measures households' loss of purchasing power and is therefore the right figure for your household budget. The core rate measures domestic price pressure, which monetary policy can influence. If the headline rate is read as a measure of inflationary pressure, a rise in the oil price looks like a monetary policy problem. If only the core rate is considered, households' real loss is left out of account.

## From price shock to inflation

An energy shock initially raises only the price level. Whether it also raises the inflation *rate* permanently depends on further conditions. If the oil price stays at its new level in the following year, its contribution to the annual rate disappears by itself, because the higher price is then already included in the previous year's figure. The shock only becomes lasting if it propagates, that is, if higher prices lead to higher wage demands, companies pass the higher wages on and the cycle starts all over again. This [[second-round effect]] is the precondition for any wage-price spiral. What matters for price pressure is the wage per unit produced and not the wage alone.

A pay settlement of 4% with productivity growth of 1% gives 1.04 divided by 1.01 = 1.030. [[Unit labour costs]] therefore rise by around 3%. This is the only increase companies have to pass on to prices to keep their margin intact. With 4% more pay and 4% more productivity, there would be no price pressure, even though the headline “4% more pay” reads the same.

For 2026 the ECB reports moderate wage growth with rising labour productivity and long-term inflation expectations of around 2%. A wage-price spiral has therefore not got under way. For this reason, central banks responded to the energy shock with a few small rate steps and not with a long series of increases. The ECB raised the deposit facility rate twice by 0.25 percentage points (2.25% from 17 June 2026, 2.50% from 16 September 2026), the Fed once (target range 3.75-4.00%).

bloecke.titel: Headline rate and core rate in the USA 2025/26
bloecke.unter: The headline rate rises to over 4% in spring 2026, while the core rate stays at around 2.5%. So far, the shock has not fed through to prices across the board.

serien.name: Core rate excluding energy and food

bloecke.md: A supply shock shifts the price level once. It only turns into persistent inflation when expectations and wage setting confirm it. A central bank is therefore guided by the forecast and never by the current figure. According to the ECB, its decisions work with long, variable and uncertain lags, typically over several quarters to years.

## The quantity equation and its limits

The oldest explanation starts directly from the money supply. It is not wrong, but it is regularly overrated.

bloecke.erklaerung: The equation is first of all an identity and therefore cannot be wrong, because V is defined as nominal output divided by the money supply. It only becomes a theory through two additional assumptions, namely that V is stable and that Y is determined by the real economy alone. Only then does the familiar proposition follow that money supply growth passes through one for one to prices.
variablen: Money supply, in the USA usually M2
Velocity: how often a unit of money is used for purchases in a year
bloecke.beispiel: For the USA in the second quarter of 2026, V = 1.418. Each dollar of the money supply M2 therefore financed around $1.42 of output a year.

bloecke.titel: Velocity of money in the USA
bloecke.unter: The [[Velocity of money|velocity]] of the US money supply M2 fell to just over half its level between 1997 and 2020. Forecasts that consider only M and treat V as constant therefore deviate from actual developments.

bloecke.md:
The relationship between the monetary base and the money supply is not stable either. The ratio of the US money supply M2 to the monetary base, known as the money multiplier, stood at 9.2 in August 2008, fell to 2.8 by August 2014 and is 4.2 in July 2026. Over the same period the monetary base rose from $848 billion to $5,524 billion, more than sixfold, while M2 almost tripled. The multiplier is therefore not a fixed quantity.

## Different effects of bond purchases

Bond purchases swap securities for central bank reserves. Reserves are banks' balances at the central bank. They cannot leave the banking system and do not end up in current accounts as purchasing power. From the pre-crisis level of 2007 to the start of 2020, the Fed almost quintupled its balance sheet without inflation reaching its target on a lasting basis. The programme worked through bond yields and asset prices and not through consumer prices.

In 2020, what had been missing ten years earlier came into play. On the one hand, there were direct transfers to households, so the money reached people who spend it. On the other hand, supply could not keep up because of disrupted supply chains. From 2022 an energy price shock followed as well. Each of the two camps was wrong once in the process. The expectation of hyperinflation that some derived from the Fed's balance sheet in 2012 proved wrong for a decade. Observers who pointed to the jump in the money supply in 2021, by contrast, judged the direction better than the central banks' forecasts at the time did. Neither “the money supply doesn't matter” nor “the money supply is everything” works as a rule. What matters is whether the money reaches buyers who are willing to spend it and whether supply can keep up.

bloecke.md:
## Risks of deflation

Deflation is more than inflation with the sign reversed. In deflation, three mechanisms reinforce one another. First, consumers postpone purchases if they expect that, say, the washing machine will be cheaper next year. As a result, demand falls and prices with it. Second, [[debt deflation]], which Irving Fisher described in 1933, takes effect. Debts are fixed in nominal terms, but prices and incomes fall, so the real debt burden rises. If everyone tries to repay at the same time, demand falls further, and the more is repaid, the heavier the burden becomes. Third, the [[effective lower bound]] comes into play. Nominal interest rates cannot be cut arbitrarily far below zero, because cash remains an alternative.

bloecke.titel: The real interest rate at the zero bound
bloecke.md: The real interest rate is roughly equal to the nominal interest rate minus expected inflation. With a nominal rate of 0% and expected inflation of 2%, it is -2% and thus strongly expansionary. If, on the other hand, everyone expects a price change of -1%, the same nominal rate of 0% gives a real interest rate of +1%. Monetary policy then has a restrictive effect, even though easing would be needed in this situation. It therefore loses its effect precisely when it is needed most urgently. The case for an inflation target above zero rests above all on this argument.

The Nikkei 225 closed at 38,915.87 points on 29 December 1989, fell to 7,607.88 points by 28 April 2003 and, after an interim recovery, to 7,054.98 points by 10 March 2009. It only surpassed its old high again on 22 February 2024, that is, after 34 years. Asset prices fell, the debts remained, and for years companies paid down debt instead of investing. Consumer prices then hovered around zero for decades, despite zero interest rates and extensive bond purchases. Japan shows that monetary policy is not powerless, but that it finds it very hard to dissolve entrenched deflation expectations. Central banks therefore try not to get anywhere near zero in the first place.

## The rationale for the 2% target

Since the strategy review in July 2021, the ECB's target has been formulated symmetrically. The aim is 2% inflation over the medium term as measured by the HICP (Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices), and deviations above and below are regarded as equally undesirable. There are four reasons for this figure.

1. It creates a safety margin against deflation and the lower bound on interest rates. With expected inflation of 2%, a nominal interest rate of zero can produce a real interest rate of -2%; with a target of zero, this room for manoeuvre is missing.
2. Nominal wages almost never fall. In a monetary union, relative costs between the member countries must nevertheless be able to shift. With slightly positive inflation, this happens through increases of different sizes instead of through cuts.
3. Price indices tend to overstate inflation slightly, because quality improvements and substitution purchases are only partly captured. A measured 2% corresponds to slightly less in real terms.
4. A known, stable target anchors expectations. This is a central bank's cheapest channel of influence, because it requires no rate rise.

The figure itself is a convention and not a constant derived from theory. It has become established internationally since the late 1980s. The target does, however, come with costs.

According to the rule of 70, purchasing power halves at 2% inflation in 70 divided by 2, that is, 35 years. The check gives 1.02 to the power of 35 = 2.00. A balance of €10,000 left for 35 years without interest ends up with the purchasing power of around €5,000, even if the central bank meets its target exactly. Central banks deliberately accept this loss of purchasing power in order to keep a distance from deflation.

The ECB projection of September 2026 gives 3.0% for 2026, 2.5% for 2027 and 2.1% for 2028. A return to target is therefore not expected until 2028. At 2.6%, the core rate is expected to be slightly above its 2026 level in 2027, because the indirect effects of the energy shock feed through with a delay. Since monetary policy only takes effect with a lag of several quarters, a central bank's rate decision answers the question of where inflation will be in two years if it does nothing, and not the question of what inflation is today. In the specialist debate, it is disputed whether a higher target of 3% or 4% would create more room for interest rate cuts in future crises. The main argument against it is that a target that is changed as soon as it becomes hard to meet no longer anchors expectations.

For your own investments, this does not lead to drastic conclusions, but it does give a clear order of questions. The question of the current inflation rate is not one of them. The first thing to clarify is whether this is a one-off jump in the level or a self-sustaining process. Next comes the question of whether long-term expectations remain anchored, and finally how high the nominal interest rate is relative to expected, not past, inflation. A decade of inflation close to zero was a historical exception and not a permanent state of the system.

begriffe.text: The passing on of a one-off price shock to wages and from there back to prices. Without a second-round effect, a shock remains a one-off jump in the level; with one, it becomes a self-sustaining process.

Labour costs per unit produced; their change roughly equals wage growth minus productivity growth. They, and not the size of the pay settlement, determine how much price pressure a wage round creates.

Mechanism described by Irving Fisher in 1933, in which falling prices and incomes increase the real burden of debts fixed in nominal terms. Simultaneous attempts to repay depress demand and thus prices further.

The interest rate level below which a central bank cannot cut the nominal interest rate any further, because cash is available as an interest-free alternative. With negative inflation expectations, the real interest rate remains positive at this point, and monetary policy loses its most important instrument.
